doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: Discovering Bill Evans through Mundell Lowe and the first trio record
summary: Mundell Lowe's phone demo led Keepnews to Evans in Village clubs and his first trio record with Motian and Kottick.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Cannonball Adderley: the sound, the man, the band

blocks.x: You were, according to Gene Lees, I believe said you were the biggest Bill Evans nut he ever knew.

Probably. Probably. I heard Bill Evans, this I guess is a story that’s been told often but it’s worth telling again. I first heard Bill Evans under the most wrong circumstances imaginable. One of the first artists that Riverside got involved with was Mundell Lowe, and Mundell — who is still alive and well and an excellent guitarist — but was very much a part of a very white jazz scene of that time. But he had known Bill back at — what is it, northeast or southeast or whatever Louisiana College, the small educational organization that Bill went to college at, Mundell was there. And so that Mundell was one of the few people that Bill knew in New York when Bill was first on the scene. And Mundell was tremendously impressed with him. And they were very close. I think Mundell explained it they had the same psychiatrist. But one day the phone rang at the Riverside offices and Mundell wanted me and Bill Grauer both to get on the phone at the same time, and he proceeded to play a tape of a piano player he wanted us to be interested in. Well first of all as a professional musician he damn well should have known better than to in effect play a demo tape over the telephone. I mean come on. The quality control at AT&T was even worse than it is now. So it wasn’t a matter of oh boy, that’s the greatest piano player I ever heard, I’ve got to get him, it was, despite all the crap, I’m hearing enough there that I want to hear more. This guy is pretty impressive. And so I went to a couple of these funky clubs in Greenwich Village where Bill was playing in quartets with somebody like Tony Scott or Don Elliot and got to know Bill, and eventually was able to persuade Bill that he should go in to the studio and make a record, which he was not terribly inclined to do. He put together a trio because Paul Motian, and I’ll digress in a minute about the name of that drummer, Paul, and then the bass player was Teddy Kottick. And we went in and did a basically trio record with a few unaccompanied solo things including the first recording of “Waltz for Debby.” And I happened to — and here’s the interesting point. Bill Evans, as a player, even though stylistically in the beginning there was a lot more bop in him than there was, then it very quickly got to be.
